utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kremer. The Appeals Chamber is sitting today to hear the parties' submissions in relation to the appeal filed by the Office of the Prosecution against the judgement acquitting Sefer Halilovic. Before I give the floor to the parties, I will briefly summarize the proceedings in this case and summarize the grounds of appeal raised before the Appeals Chamber in this case as well as the way we are going to proceed over these two afternoons. In its judgement handed down on the 16th of November, 2005, the Trial Chamber, Trial Chamber I, made up of Judges Liu, presiding the Chamber; Judge Mumba and Judge El Mahdi, found Sefer Halilovic not guilty of the one count he was charged with; i.e., murder, a violation of the laws or customs of war, under Articles 3 and 7(3) of the Statute. Mr. Halilovic was acquitted of all charges and he was immediately released. The OTP has appealed the Trial Chamber's judgement rendered on 16th November 2005. In support of its request for the judgement to be reversed, the Prosecution has raised four grounds of appeal which I will now summarize. Under its first ground of appeal, the Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber has erred in law and in fact in finding that the Prosecution had not proven beyond reasonable doubt that Sefer Halilovic was the superior of the perpetrators of the crimes committed in Grabovica. The first ground of appeal consists of six subgrounds alleging errors of law and fact. Under the first subground, the Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber has erred in applying the legal standard required to demonstrate effective control. Under the second subground, the Prosecution alleges that the Trial Chamber erred in requiring the Prosecution to prove not only that there was a military operation, but that this operation was called Operation Neretva. Under its third subground, the Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber erred in requiring the Prosecution to prove that the location in which the inspection team was accommodated was an advanced command post from which the military operation mentioned earlier on was commanded. Under its fourth subground, the Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber erred in using the fact that Sefer Halilovic had not taken the necessary and reasonable steps to punish the perpetrators of the crimes committed in Grabovica, to support the finding that he did not have the material ability to punish the perpetrators of these crimes. Under its fifth subground, the Prosecution alleges that the Trial Chamber erred in applying the beyond reasonable proof standard. Under its sixth and final subground, the Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber erred in refusing to admit a statement made by Sefer Halilovic in 1996. Under its second ground of appeal, the Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber erred in law in failing to consider and make findings of fact on whether Sefer Halilovic knew or had reason to know that criminal acts were about to be committed in Grabovica. Under its third ground of appeal, the Prosecution argues that the Trial Chamber erred in law in distinguishing between a general obligation and a specific obligation to prevent crimes under Article 7(3) of the Statute. Finally, under its fourth and final ground of appeal, the Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber erred in law in failing to admit the report and hear the testimony of Major-General Andrew Ridgway as a military expert witness. As for Mr. Halilovic, he argues that the appeal lodged by the Prosecution should be dismissed summarily. Alternatively, he requests the Appeals Chamber to dismiss all grounds of appeal of the Prosecution on the merits. During the hearing the parties may make their submissions on the grounds and subgrounds of the appeal in the order they see fit. However, I would like to remind the Prosecution and counsel for Mr. Halilovic that they were invited to address a number of issues that were listed in the addendum to the Scheduling Order of 19 June 2006. I'm not going to repeat all these points now. Pursuant to Article 25 of the Statute, the appellant should restrict his submissions to errors on questions of law invalidating the decision and errors of fact which have occasioned a miscarriage of justice. As you know, an appeal is not a de novo trial and the appellant may not merely repeat the arguments made at trial. Furthermore, the appellant is under the obligation to provide specific reference to the authorities supporting his submissions on appeal. This hearing will proceed according to the Scheduling Order issued on the 4th of June, 2007. The representatives of the OTP will have one hour and 30 minutes to make their submissions. We'll then have a 20-minute break. Following the break, the representatives of the OTP will be able to make further submissions during 45 minutes. The Defence will then be able to start responding for 45 minutes. We'll then adjourn until tomorrow, 2.15 p.m. It would prove extremely useful for the Appeals Chamber for the parties to make their submissions in a clear, concise, and orderly manner. I would like to inform the parties that at any time the Judges may interrupt their submissions to put questions if they feel that it is necessary or the Judges may raise issues following each one of the presentations. If you have no questions or comments about the way we are going to proceed, I would now like to ask the Prosecution to make its submissions. Mr. Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, I will address you on the first and second grounds of appeal as well as question one, two, three, and five in the addendum to the Scheduling Order. Mr. Buck will address you on ground number 3 of the grounds of appeal, and Ms. Baig will answer question 7. We will save for reply, if necessary, the answers to questions 4 and 6 which were directed at the -- at Mr. Halilovic. Let me begin by assisting the Court and giving you an overview as to how my argument will proceed. My argument has six parts. The first part will be the answer to the first question addressing de facto commander; the second part will be a short factual overview; the third part, and the main part, is the discussion of the legal error, and during this discussion I propose to answer questions 3 and question 5; part four is a discussion of the application of the correct legal standard to the evidence, and during that discussion I will answer question 2; part five is a discussion of the second and third elements of superior responsibility under Article 7(3); and part six is our concluding submission that Sefer Halilovic should be convicted of the crimes for which he was charged. Let me begin by answering the question of de facto commander, question 1 of the questions posed by the Bench. The question was: Has the de facto commander issue in the notice of appeal been abandoned? The answer is: No. Where in the appeal brief are the references found? That is the second question. In the introduction to ground 1 of the Prosecution appeal brief, the Prosecution states that Halilovic was de facto commander of the operation. In the appeal brief, paragraph 2.3, we submit: "Thus, according to Halilovic's superior to Halilovic's subordinate to Halilovic's inspection team and to Halilovic himself, Halilovic was the de jure or de facto commander." As it is briefed in paragraph 2.10, the term "superior" includes military commander. So every time the appeal brief refers to Halilovic's de facto superior position, it includes de facto command. De facto superior is used in paragraphs 2.11, 2.23, 2.47, 2.50, 2.52, 2.59, 2.83, 2.86, 2.94, and 2.98 and is implicit in 2.15. This appeal is about a single issue: Effective control. Effective control, and not command, is the only requirement to establish a superior/subordinate relationship in the context of Article 7(3) responsibility. This is why the core of the Prosecution's argument is on effective control and superior position instead of de facto command. And this is reflected in the notice of appeal at paragraphs 3 and 4(i). In conclusion, the Prosecution's position is that Halilovic was the de facto commander of the operation, but in any event he had effective control over those who committed the crimes. The Prosecution has not abandoned this position. A short factual overview helps put the legal argument in perspective. The facts of this case involve the murder of 13 civilians in Grabovica on the 8th and 9th of September, 1993. ABiH soldiers, including the 9th Brigade subordinate to Halilovic, murdered them. Halilovic was the chief of the Main Staff of the Supreme Command of the ABiH and the second highest-ranking member of the army. Between 30 August and 20 September 1993, Halilovic was also the leader of an inspection team coordinating combat operations in the Neretva valley to end the HVO blockade of Mostar. Four army corps and several independent units of the ABiH contributed men, materiel, munitions, and technical support to the operation. The inspection team structure was used because a temporary operations command had not proven effective in the past. As inspection team leader, Halilovic issued orders assembling soldiers, materiel, munitions, and technical support for the planned offensive, billeting resubordinated soldiers, directing combat responsibility and preparedness, initiating combat action, and so on. Halilovic ordered the resubordination of 9th Brigade soldiers from Sarajevo for combat, aware of their previous violent criminal behaviour. Halilovic refused requests for the return of troops to their home units until the operation ended. Halilovic was the superior of the perpetrators when the crimes were committed and immediately after. Halilovic failed to take any steps to prevent the risk of violence to civilians in Grabovica by the soldiers of the 9th Brigade, which resulted in seven of the 13 murders, even though he was on notice of the real and reasonable risk of future crimes by the troops. Halilovic learned of the Grabovica murders on the 9th of September and failed to take reasonable and necessary measures to punish the ABiH perpetrators. Sefer Halilovic should have been convicted as a superior pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute for the murders committed by his subordinates in Grabovica. He was acquitted not because of lack of evidence but because the Trial Chamber made a fundamental legal error in applying Article 7(3). The legal error was not -- in not applying the correct legal standard to establish a superior/subordinate relationship under the first element of superior responsibility under 7(3). The correct legal standard under the first element is effective control over the subordinates who committed the crimes. The Trial Chamber correctly set out the correct legal standard when describing the applicable legal principles at trial judgement 57 to 63. However, when applying its legal standard to establish this element, the Trial Chamber asked itself if Sefer Halilovic was commander of combat operations and not if he was in effective control. Halilovic had effective control over the perpetrators by virtue of his position as their de facto superior, the most senior-ranking officer in Herzegovina and leader of the inspection team of the operation in which they participated. The legal error results from the Trial Chamber applying this wrong legal standard. The application of the wrong legal standard is clear in the findings at trial judgement 371 and 372. In those two sections or paragraphs, the Trial Chamber finds reasonable doubt on the first element of superior responsibility because it was at -- because it asked itself the wrong legal question. It asked itself: Was Halilovic in overall control --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kremer, can you please slow down. The French interpreters find it difficult to follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Let me start again. The application of the wrong legal standard is clear in the findings at trial judgement paragraphs 371 and 372. The Trial Chamber finds a reasonable doubt on the first element because it asked itself the wrong legal questions. Was Halilovic in overall command of combat operations in Herzegovina, with emphasis on combat -- command of combat operations. It also asked itself this question: Was Halilovic commanding and controlling combat activities, with emphasis on commanding and controlling combat activities. And it asked itself: Was Halilovic either de jure or de facto commander of the alleged Operation Neretva? Again, with emphasis on de facto commander. This focus on overall command of combat operations, commanding and controlling combat activities, and command role of Operation Neretva permeates the entire trial judgement, particularly in paragraphs 332 to 372, which findings are re-affirmed in paragraphs 736 to 746. This narrow focus resulted in names being elevated to indispensable facts: The name of the operation, Operation Neretva, and the name in formal existence of a forward command post, the IKM to be proven beyond a reasonable doubt. This is fully briefed in our appeal brief at 2.42 to 2.16, and I will not go into it in detail. Question 3 of the Chamber's questions asks: How would a finding on the existence of an IKM in Jablanica have led to a de facto superior finding? The answer is that this finding alone would not have had this result. However, the existence of an IKM or operational command post used by Halilovic is an indicator of effective control which can support a positive finding of de facto superior. Moving now to question 5. It is true that the Ntagerura case or in the Ntagerura case decided by this Chamber a similarly worded ground of appeal dealing with beyond reasonable doubt was dismissed by the ICTR Appeals Chamber. However, this dismissal was only because the Appeals Chamber found that the Trial Chamber properly evaluated the evidence. In this case the Trial Chamber evaluated the evidence using the wrong legal standard. This is why the Prosecution relies on the finding in Ntagerura on how the evidence should be evaluated. Just moving to paragraph 174 of the Ntagerura Appeals Chamber judgement very briefly quoting from two parts of that paragraph. "The assessment of credibility of the relevant evidence cannot be undertaken by a piecemeal approach. Individual items of evidence have to be analysed in light of the entire body of evidence adduced. The standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt is applied to establish the facts forming the elements of the crime and the form of responsibility alleged against the accused as well as with respect to the -- with respect for the facts which are indispensable for entering a conviction." In this case the Trial Chamber committed the very two errors warned against in Ntagerura. First, it considered individual pieces of evidence piecemeal; and second, it then applied the beyond reasonable standard to them individually, notwithstanding that they were not elements of the crime or modes of responsibility or indispensable. Examples of both errors include the Trial Chamber's assessment of the existence of an IKM and the name: Operation Neretva. On the piecemeal complaint, the Trial Chamber examined individual orders and events in isolation in determining de facto commander of combat operations. The evidence was simply not considered as a whole. As we set out in our reply, the Prosecution agrees with and relies on the principles articulated by the ICTR Appeals Chamber in Ntagerura. The judgement actually explains how and why the Trial Chamber went astray. The Trial Chamber cites the wording of the indictment as its rationale for making command of combat operations its exclusive focus; however, on a plain reading of the indictment the Prosecution's case against Halilovic was never based solely on his overall command and commanding and controlling combat activities or operations, nor was the Prosecution case based solely on his being de jure or de facto commander of combat operations in Herzegovina. To the contrary, the Prosecution case always included a case of effective control beyond command. And I refer you to our appeals brief, paragraphs 2.17 to 2.26 for a fuller discussion on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Kremer, it would be useful on this point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Judge Meron has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It would be useful on that point if you were to refer us not to that point made in your arguments during or briefs during -- on the appeal, but in your arguments before the Trial Chamber. I must say that I had the impression that during the trial you only pled a tier of effective control based on command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: If I could answer that question in a moment. I'll get the references and I'll deal with that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll finish my point on indictment and hopefully we'll have the answer. By misreading the indictment, focusing on formal military command structure and command of combat operations and applying a reasonable doubt standard to dispensable facts, the Trial Chamber fell foul of the concluding sentence in paragraph 254 of the Celebici appeal judgement: "Concepts of subordination, hierarchy, and chains of command need not be established in the sense of formal organisational structures so long as the fundamental requirement of an effective power to control the subordinate in the sense of preventing and punishing criminal conduct is satisfied." The indictment alleged command of combat operations as among the facts from which to determine effective control, but the Prosecution's case did not depend on them, nor were these facts elements of the offence or elements of the mode of liability or indispensable facts. In the trial judgement the Trial Chamber's overly formalistic approach to its analysis of effective control is striking. This is particularly evident in paragraphs 363 to 371. But it also pervades other parts of the trial judgement wherein evidence is being summarized. A close examination of these paragraphs demonstrates that the Trial Chamber looked again and again for combat -- command responsibility in a formal military sense. It looked for formal appointment, it looked for formal military title, and it looked for defined military command roles. But the search for formality was dubious, as the evidence showed that the ABiH did not operate fully as a mature army. Thus, the exclusive search for these indicia was bound to fail as it did. There was no formal appointment of anyone to the role of and with the title of commander of Operation Neretva. Instead, Delic assigned a team of senior officers from the Main Staff under the leadership of Halilovic, his Chief of Staff. The inspection team under Halilovic had a large measure of control over all of the corps and individual units assigned to the operation. The proof of Halilovic's control as inspection team leader lay in his actions and the actions of those he controlled, and not on his formal appointment as commander. The Trial Chamber overlooked that the case pleaded in the indictment rested on the authority and power vested in Halilovic through his role and function as de facto superior, as senior officer in Herzegovina for the operation, and as team leader of the inspection team. Instead, the Trial Chamber applied the wrong legal standard focusing solely on de jure indicators of command -- of command of combat operations and demanding proof beyond a reasonable doubt of a formal appointment, of a formal title, of a formal role confirming that Halilovic was commander of combat operations. This Chamber in Celebici accepted the Celebici Trial Chamber's reasoning that: "The actual exercise of authority in the absence of formal appointment is sufficient for the purpose of incurring criminal responsibility, provided the superior exercises actual power of control," paragraph 206. This focus on formal military hierarchy and command of combat operations caused the Trial Chamber to ignore the effectiveness of the inspection team's structure. In assigning Halilovic as inspection team leader, Delic insured a senior and experienced military presence and control over ABiH soldiers on the ground. This is borne out by the evidence that will be discussed shortly. The section factual findings as to the status of Sefer Halilovic during Operation Neretva, paragraphs 363 to 372, is a good example of the wrong approach taken by the Trial Chamber. The section concludes with the finding that Halilovic was not de jure or de facto commander of the alleged operation. Indeed, the analysis made by the Trial Chamber in this section is only focused on de jure command. The Trial Chamber only looked for formal military titles and military roles, and on this sole basis concluded that Halilovic was not de facto commander. Moreover, the Trial Chamber failed to take into account facts that showed de jure command on the basis of the absence of de jure command. Two examples illustrate this argument. First, at paragraph 366, the Trial Chamber dismissed evidence of lower-ranking soldiers that they considered Sefer Halilovic to be their commander and of Bakir Alispahic, the minister of interior, who assumed that Sefer Halilovic was commander of Operation Neretva. And they dismissed this evidence because Halilovic did not have a formal appointment. Second, at paragraph 380, the Trial Chamber failed to acknowledge Halilovic's exercise of actual authority and power through Halilovic's issuance of orders, even though it accepted that Halilovic issued orders within the framework of the orders initially issued by Rasim Delic. Halilovic issued orders. Halilovic's orders flowed down to the corps and unit commanders. The corps and unit commanders followed these orders with the corps and unit command orders cascading down to brigade commanders and so on. As previously said, Halilovic's orders covered movement of personnel, materiel, and supplies, combat matters, et cetera. Halilovic's orders were issued, implemented, and reported on. The consequence of the Trial Chamber's formalistic approach of looking exclusively on command of combat operations and using isolated examples of orders not immediately complied with in strict military fashion as evidence of lack of command was that a multitude of Halilovic's implemented orders were considered -- or were not considered and the legal test for effective control was never properly applied. This is what caused the acquittal of Sefer Halilovic. Formalism also allowed the Trial Chamber to find ambiguity in command of combat operations because of the lack of military discipline within the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to use lack of discipline to support its negative findings on effective control. But these examples of lack of discipline do not disprove effective control. While they may be relevant to test the effectiveness of control, the more important question is whether these orders were, in fact, followed. In all of the examples cited by the Trial Chamber in trial judgement 743 to 745, they were. The Blaskic appeals judgement at paragraph 69 tells us that the indicators of effective control are more a matter of evidence than of substantive law, and those indicators are limited to showing that the accused had the power to prevent, punish, or initiate measures leading to proceedings against the alleged perpetrators where appropriate. Thus, the critical question that the Trial Chamber should have endeavoured to answer is whether Halilovic had the material ability to prevent, punish, or initiate measures leading to proceedings against the Grabovica perpetrators. It never asked that question. Because the Trial Chamber acquitted Halilovic based on the application of an incorrect legal standard under the first element of superior responsibility under the Blaskic test, the Appeals Chamber will have to apply the correct legal standard to the evidence based on its review of the trial record, in this case, the facts and evidence cited in the trial judgement and the briefs. Although the ultimate determination of the impugned legal question was based on facts, this is not a case where full deference to the factual determinations of the Trial Chamber can be given because the error on the first element permeates the entire judgement and no factual findings or limited factual findings were made on the other two elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Before I leave this area and move on to an assessment of the facts, I'd like to address Judge Pocar's -- Judge Meron's question, I'm sorry. The answer to your question I think can be simply found in our appeal brief at paragraph 216 which makes reference to the Prosecution closing brief at paragraph 142 to 186. If I could, I would just like to read that paragraph because I think it clearly points out what the Prosecution's position is. "The charges contained in the indictment elaborated in the pre-trial brief and Prosecution's opening statement and maintained in the Prosecution closing brief go well beyond the narrow issue of command determined by the Trial Chamber. Having found that Halilovic was not the formal or de jure commander of Operation Neretva, the Trial Chamber had a duty to continue its inquiry and to determine whether he nevertheless had superior authority over the perpetrators because he was the most senior ABiH officer in the region and because he was the team leader of the inspection team. The Trial Chamber's findings -- or failure to make necessary findings constitutes an error of law invalidating the judgement." The Prosecution appeal brief, as I said, has over 40 paragraphs dealing with the issue -- the issue of the basis upon which the Prosecution alleges; that Sefer Halilovic was the superior of the subordinates who committed the murders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I don't know Mr. Kremer at this point in time how satisfied I am by this answer, but I would like to ask the Defence team in due course to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I'm now going to move to part four of my submissions, the application of the correct legal standard to the facts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kremer, before moving on to another topic, I have a simple question to put to you. You mentioned the authority beyond any formal appointment; in other words, you attributed to Sefer Halilovic an authority outside or beyond the scope of any formal appointment. Now, if we speak in terms of a military hierarchy, anybody having an authority outside any formal appointment, how could this be or how could this operate? Would you be so kind as to expand on this, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: It must be remembered that Mr. Halilovic was at the time the former commander of the army. He was Chief of Staff of the Main Staff of the Supreme Command of the army. He was second in command, as it were, of the army hierarchy, and the placement of a person in his position in the field for an operation makes him the highest-ranking officer present at the operation. And in military terms, if he gives an order, it must be followed. There was ample evidence in the record where Sefer Halilovic, as head of the inspection team, as the highest-ranking officer in the area, or Sefer Halilovic, as de facto commander, gave an order and it was followed. A formal appointment is unnecessary in the circumstances to find de facto control -- or effective control, I'm sorry. And as I go through the facts, I hope to highlight some very good examples of situations from which it can be inferred that -- and the only inference is or the only conclusion will be that Sefer Halilovic was in command. Our position is quite simply that Sefer Halilovic acted as though he had command. He believed he had command. Rasim Delic confirmed in several respects that he had command, both by order and by statement. And the actions of Sefer Halilovic in issuing orders throughout the period for a variety of tasks confirmed that it was Sefer Halilovic who was in charge of the combat operation. He did not have the formal title of commander of Operation Neretva, but he did not have to have it in order to make a finding that he's responsible for the crimes of the soldiers who worked for him and executed the operation that he had responsibility for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nonetheless, to qualify authority you did quote a number of people who had been formally appointed. What I would like to know, given that you stressed on the authority of this person who had not been formally appointed, is such an -- such authority consistent with no formal appointment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: We say it is, Your Honour, and I -- and I say this because Rasim Delic said that Sefer Halilovic was in charge. The Commander-in-Chief of the army, and I'll deal with this evidence in a while, said on at least two occasions, Sefer Halilovic was in charge. He issued orders that certainly confirmed that he is in charge. The Court found some ambiguity in that -- in that order, but when one takes the order and takes the actions that Sefer Halilovic takes as a result of that order and take the position of Delic, the supreme commander, and look at Sefer Halilovic's admissions about his role in the operation, one has to start from the context of: He is in command. Whether he's appointed formally or not, he is in de facto command of that operation. Whether it's as inspection team leader, whether it's because he's the highest-ranking officer, all of the facts point to the conclusion that he was in command. And what the Trial Chamber did is they turned the facts on their head by looking for formal command in absence and then they looked at the facts that addressed only de jure command. But all of the facts dealing with de facto command, if looked at properly, establish beyond any reasonable doubt that Sefer Halilovic was the commander of this operation. And in respect of the troops of the 9th Brigade, he issued an order to the 1st Corps commander to have the troops resubordinated. He, when the troops arrived, refused to let them go back. The only conclusion you can come to by -- from those two events is that Sefer Halilovic had control over those troops, and there are other examples. There are many other examples to show the degree of his authority, control, and power. And we can see, there is no formal appointment. There is a formal appointment as inspection team leader, and from that can flow effective control over the operation, but that isn't the question. The real question is, looking at the time and the place and the troops who committed the crime, because Sefer Halilovic was there, in charge -- there as part of the operation, did he or was he the superior of those subordinates? He was the superior, otherwise he could not have taken the actions he did in respect of them. He couldn't have got materiel to supply them for the combat operation. He couldn't have ordered these people to be brought -- to come to the Neretva valley for combat operations. He couldn't have said to the 1st Corps commander: You can't have your men back. The facts, I think, tell -- answer the question. If you can focus on de jure control and de jure command, you will get to the same place the Trial Chamber got to. But our submission, with respect, is that one shouldn't start from that location; one should simply say: There was no de jure appointment here. Let us look at the facts and find out what we conclude based on those facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Shahabuddeen would like to put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kremer, I would like to make sure that I'm understanding the case you are putting forward. As I appreciated, you're saying this, that what the Prosecution had to prove to the Trial Chamber was that Mr. Halilovic exercised effective control over the assailants, shall we say. But what the Trial Chamber did was to focus on his formal position in relation to combat operations. Now, I gather that you are saying that outside of formal combat operations, there was evidence on which the Trial Chamber could have found that Mr. Halilovic exercised effective authority over the assailants; you have just mentioned one, that he declined to send back certain troops. But could it be this, that your presentation in the Trial Chamber led the Trial Chamber to believe that your thesis that Mr. Halilovic exercised effective control over the assailants really turned on his having overall control in relation to combat operations so that the Trial Chamber would have answered the first question as to whether Mr. Halilovic had effective control by reference to whether he had overall control in relation to formal combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I take a careful -- or I would submit, in fact. I don't think because I know is that the indictment, the pre-trial brief, and the closing brief all address the three opportunities for finding effective control. They raise the de facto command element, they raise the highest position in Herzegovina, and they raise the inspection team leadership of the operation. The case of the Prosecution never was focused form on -- on who commanded Operation Neretva exclusively. That certainly was the focus because the criminal liability resulted from him being placed in that theatre of war for a very brief period of time, and the crimes were committed during that episode -- that might not be the right word to describe it. And so obviously there had to be a focus. There had to be a focus on who he was, what he was doing, how it was done, what happened. But the fundamental question to be asked by the Trial Chamber, whether it was clearly articulated or not - and I submit that it was clearly articulated in the indictment, in the pre-trial brief, in the final trial brief - that the case of the Prosecution was effective control beyond command; it was a de facto superior case because there was no formal appointment. That was apparent to everybody when this case started. And to say that a formal appointment was required before you could convict Sefer Halilovic, then everybody has wasted their time for all those months. The Prosecution's case was Sefer Halilovic was there, he acted in accordance with Delic's order, he did several things, multiple tasks, throughout the 20-plus-day period in which he subordinated troops, he assembled materiel and munitions, he developed battle plans, he instructed various commanders on how and where they were to go to battle and when, he issued orders that they should go into battle, and he refused to let people go while the battle was still ongoing. And he has all of the trappings of a commander except he doesn't have the title. But because he doesn't have the title, it doesn't mean that he isn't the de facto commander, that he isn't in charge. And Delic was saying when questioned by the 1st Corps -- the deputy commander of the 1st Corps, Karevelic: Do I have to follow this order to send the 9th Brigade and the 10th Brigade to Halilovic, and Delic says: Yes, follow the order. And that's in the transcript or in the judgement. And I'll get to these examples, but the judgement is replete with examples as to how effective control is proven and effective control is established through the evidence, through Halilovic's own words, through Halilovic's actions, through Delic's words and Delic's actions. And it's confirmed by the views of the people who were following those orders. And it is throughout the whole spectrum of what is going on on the ground during Operation Neretva. And what the Defence did in this case is made a lot of smoke about de jure command, and unfortunately the Trial Chamber accepted the fact that if there's -- there's no formal title, there's no formal role defined, and so on, that there must be a reasonable doubt as to his role as commander, and therefore there was no effective control, but that was the wrong question. They -- the question that was being asked of the Trial Chamber by the indictment and in the briefs from the Prosecution was: Decide this case on effective control. And it was not decided on effective control. And that's why we're here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I'm a little unclear as to the distinction which you are making between effective control and overall control of the combat operations. Are you sure that it ceases of effective control cannot include the question whether Mr. Halilovic had any formal positions in relation to combat operations? I gathered from something else you might have said that, yes, the first proposition can include the second proposition, but what the Trial Chamber did was that it focused on the second proposition only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes, that is our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I think, given our discussion, it is perhaps helpful for me to move into the application of the correct legal standard to the facts, because the position being advanced by the Prosecution, if you accept that there was a -- an error in the legal standard that was applied, applying the correct legal standard to the evidence, we say that a conviction will result. And I will go through and demonstrate why that is so. I'll look at, and I've already forecast this in my answers to your questions, five different areas. One is Halilovic's admissions of control; Halilovic's material ability to control the troops; Halilovic's material ability to give orders that were followed by subordinates; Halilovic's material ability to initiate an investigation or measures leading to proceedings; and Delic's statements on Halilovic's authority and power. And at the end of the review of my facts, I will answer question 2, how the inspection team functions could be an indicator of effective control over the perpetrators. First, Halilovic admitted that he was in control over the perpetrators. In Exhibit 130, an inspection team report dated 20 September, Halilovic made a contemporaneous admission. This exhibit is co-signed by Halilovic and three team members and is sent to the Presidency, Delic, the minister of the interior, the defence ministry, and the Executive Board of the SDA. In his letter to the president, which is Exhibit 498, Halilovic states: "I submitted in a report," referring to that report, so he takes credit for the report. In the inspection team report, Halilovic and the other three team members admit to: One, being in the field from 29 August to 19 September; two, establishing contacts with the 3rd, 4th, and 6th Corps; three, setting up forward command post in Jablanica with the aim of coordinating and executing combat operations; four, planning the operation and ensuring logistical means for the operation; five, operating under Delic's order and estimating the combat-readiness of the commands and units and to leading combat operations; and six, having successfully coordinated combat operations with the units of the 6th Corps. Two very telling documents replete with admissions as to his role in the operation are Halilovic's letter to President Izetbegovic dated May 1995, which is Exhibit 498, as I already mentioned, and a chapter from Halilovic's book "Cunning Strategy," published in 1999, and that's found in Exhibit 281. The book and the letter are very similar in content and can only be read in one way. The person in control of the operation was Halilovic. His admissions of leadership, control, power, and authority leap off the pages. In addition to these three documents, I want to remind the Chamber of subground 6 of ground 1 relating to the 1996 statement of Halilovic which was, in the Prosecution's submission, erroneously not admitted. A positive decision on this issue would add other admissions. Halilovic admits that he kept Delic informed, but his words are very clear. It was he, Halilovic, and his team that did the work to conceive, plan, prepare, and have approved the combat plans for the operation, then to implement carry them out and monitor their execution. The Trial Chamber did find that under the command of Rasim Delic the re-organisation and resubordination of troops was carried out. It also found that Halilovic implemented the orders of Delic, in keeping with his role as team leader of the inspection team, charged with coordinating and monitoring functions. I pose the question: How could Halilovic carry out orders if he was not subordinated to carry out those orders? And if his orders are directed to the corps commanders or unit commanders, do they have to follow Halilovic or do they have to wait for an order of Delic? The evidence shows that it was Halilovic's orders that were given to the corps commanders, Halilovic's orders that went to the unit commanders, and Halilovic -- it was Halilovic's orders that were followed by them during the course of the operation, not those of Delic. In these admissions Halilovic describes how he performed his role and functions of inspection team leader. In the Prosecution's submission, likes -- he performed them like a superior with effective control over his subordinates. These admissions were never considered in their proper context. When one evaluates Halilovic's admissions against contemporaneous documents and events, his conclusions as to how he performed his role are confirmed. In addition, Halilovic had the power to order troops to join the operation, to direct and control them when they arrived, and to decide when they could return to their home unit. One example of control Halilovic had over the troops involved the operation -- involved in the operation is illustrated by his resubordinating troops. On 2 September 1993, Halilovic ordered 1st Corps to: "Prepare Delta Brigade, 9th and 10th Brigade, and Colakovic's unit, totaling over 300 soldiers, with full sets of weapons and equipment, and send them no later than Friday evening, 3 September 1993, to Bradina where the 6th Corps will take them," and that's Exhibit 161. And as I've mentioned already, Karevelic, the deputy commander of the 1st Corps expressed concern about resubordination of troops from the 1st Corps. He calls Delic, who confirmed that Karavelic should act in accordance with Halilovic's order, and that's found in judgement paragraphs 232, 233, and 235. These three paragraphs, when studied with the exhibit, confirm that Halilovic had the power to subordinate troops -- subordinate troops for combat operations, and Delic confirmed it. Another example of the material ability to control troops begins when Halilovic met Karavelic and subordinate commanders to discuss sending 2nd Independent Battalion troops to combat. And these troops had not been mentioned in the 2 September order. That's referred to in judgement paragraphs 236 to 237. On the 6th of September, Karavelic implemented Halilovic's order, that is Exhibit 161, and ordered the 2nd Independent Commander to prepare and send a company of 100 to 120 soldiers for that day. The companies were to carry out the assignment for no longer than seven days. And I should point out that in judgement paragraph 7 -- 276 which discusses this point, the exhibit is referred to as Exhibit 123. There is an error. Our review suggests that the exhibit number correctly is 385. And the story continues. On September 8th Halilovic chaired a reporting session meeting in Konjic and resubordinated the 2nd, the 9th, and the 10th Brigades, and that's trial judgement 291 and trial judgement 423. But the proof of the material ability to control these troops comes starting on the 12th of September when there are a series of requests made to Halilovic by the commander of the 1st Corps; by Karavelic, the deputy commander; and by the 2nd Battalion commander, to allow the withdrawal of their troops back to Sarajevo. And that's found at Exhibit 338 -- 388, Exhibit 272, and trial judgement paragraphs 304 and 423. All of these requests were denied. The 2nd Independent Battalion, in fact, stayed until 19 September, the end of the operation, and that's found at judgement 306. So it is clear from that scenario that not only could Halilovic select the troops he wanted, he could order them to come, and he could ensure that they stayed for the duration of the engagement. Associated with the task of troop movement and troop --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kremer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry for interrupting you. Judge Shahabuddeen has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kremer, you said all these requests were denied. May I ask, denied by whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: They were made to Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: They were denied by him?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: The -- the evidence is, at least from the 1st Corps commander and by Karavelic, they were denied by him, I believe. Karavelic I think said he asked and Sefer Halilovic denied, yes. Associated with the task of troop movement and troop resubordination is accommodating the troops in the combat zone. In this regard, Halilovic could also make decisions concerning billeting of troops and allocating lodging. Halilovic personally participated in searching for billeting sites on the 3rd of September, that's in judgement paragraph 251 and in paragraphs 281, 82 to 290. These examples show that Halilovic had the power to order troops to join the operation, as I've said, and when they joined he could tell them where they were to stay. Halilovic also had the ability -- material ability to give orders that were followed. The trial judgement's conclusion suggest that Halilovic and the inspection team were powerless appendages to the corps and units involved in Operation Neretva; however, the evidence it cites to support its findings actually established the opposite. The planned combat operation involving three corps and independent units required central control, central control to develop, implement, direct, carry out and monitor the operational and plan. Central control was needed because this was an important and strategic operation critical to Mostar and potentially affecting the security of Sarajevo. The inspection team was appointed the body to perform these functions, Halilovic was his leader, and he performed his role by issuing orders. As the previous examples already have demonstrated, the trial judgement contains multiple examples where Halilovic issued orders to subordinates that were followed. A very good example relates to the implementation of the plan of action for combat. On September 4th, Halilovic, Delic, and others met at the Zulfikar base where the operation, plan of action, and working map were approved and signed by Delic and Halilovic, judgement 258, 268 and 69. The map became the working map for the briefings with all corps and unit commanders in preparation for combat, and the map is Exhibit 131. Beginning on September 5th, Halilovic chaired a series of meetings with different commanders and their subordinate officers to issue specific tasks to the participating units and the subordinate officers accepted assignments. I refer you to trial judgement paragraphs 264 to 267, 291 and 292, 294 and 296. The commanders were ordered to wait for a signal to go into battle. Halilovic gave a coded signal on 12th September for the brigades to go into action. That is in trial judgement 314. And once the battle started, commands of units sent battle reports to Halilovic, judgement 315. Another good example is the meeting at Dobro Polje on 5 September, where Halilovic assigned the 6th Corps to capture the area of Crni Vrh and Makljen. This is found in paragraph 265. In the 6th Corps command order to attack of 11 September 1993, Exhibit 152, it is stated: "I have decided to go on attack on a particular axis in order to destroy the enemy in the general Crni Vrh sector as the primary task and then to continue with offensive combat operations to take control of the Makljen feature." So that the order issued by the 6th Corps command to attack is on the same specific terms as Halilovic assigned it the day before -- six days before. A third example of Halilovic's material ability can be found in the relationship between Exhibit 501, in which Halilovic gives tactical orders directing the 317th Brigade and Exhibit 150, which is an order from the commander of the 317, giving specific directions to his troops on the basis of Halilovic's order and a subsequent order of the 6th command. And that's referred to in judgement 322. So from start to finish Sefer Halilovic is issuing orders to subordinate commanders and those subordinate commanders are following his orders. His orders are being re-issued -- not re-issued, are being followed by orders issued by the subordinate commanders down to brigade commanders and on down, depending on the responsibility being directed to the smaller units. Halilovic accepted that he had the material ability to punish his subordinates for crimes, and this is perhaps the most important discussion of material ability because it focuses directly on the effective control test. On September 9th, when Alispahic, the minister of the interior, called the IKM to advise Halilovic of the events in Grabovica, he said -- or he also said to Halilovic that the events should be investigated and that other necessary measures should be taken. Halilovic responded that the case would be investigated. Alispahic advised Halilovic that there were problems and that Halilovic would have to meet them, and this is referred to in judgement paragraph 667. Later at a personal meeting with Halilovic in Jablanica, Halilovic told Alispahic that the military would resolve the problem with its own resources, that there would be no need for civilian police to interfere, and that it was possible for the perpetrators of the crime to create an incident with the policemen, warning: Don't investigate if you're civilian police. 668 is the reference to that. Halilovic did not say: I can't do anything. He did not say to Alispahic: I have no authority, I do not control them, I am not in charge of them, they are not my troops. What did he say? He said: Measures would be taken. On September 9th, Halilovic asked Dzankovic whether he had heard what had happened in Grabovica, and when he answered in the affirmative, Halilovic told him: "I want you to collect as much information as possible and send it -- and inform the Sarajevo command about it." This is Exhibit -- or Exhibit 215 and trial judgement 670. At a meeting of the officers at the IKM, it was mentioned that Karic, an inspection team member, and Halilovic had taken upon themselves the obligation of investigating the events and taking reasonable measures, trial judgement 682. But despite Halilovic's recognition of his duty to investigate and take reasonable measures in respect of the perpetrators of the Grabovica massacre, he did nothing. And these events that I've just described, the discussion with Alispahic, Zenkovic, and the discussion with the officers, all three relate to one event: The event in Grabovica. Moreover, as already mentioned, the inspection team report at 1.30 recommends criminal investigations and proceedings against various the members -- I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Vaz has a question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- A point of clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kremer, I'm sorry to interrupt you because you had already moved on to a different issue. But I would like you to give us some additional information about Dzankovic. Did he report to Halilovic with respect to the outcome of the investigation you've mentioned; and if it's the case, if that's the case, could you tell us about Halilovic's response, Halilovic's reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Dzankovic did not report to Halilovic after the inspection team concluded its affairs in the area on the 19th and wrote his report on the 20th. He wrote reports, but the reports went to the Main Staff security administration. He did not direct those reports to Halilovic, nor did Halilovic inquire as to the status of the investigation or inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: There's a specific --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Did you finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Kremer, Judge Schomburg has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Kremer, I have two legal questions. First of all, with regards to the omission to punish, what would you have expected Mr. Halilovic to do; and second, if you come to the conclusion and the Appeals Chamber would follow you in this conclusion, that he omitted to prevent the crimes, can a person be held criminally liable at the same time for not preventing and for not punishing? Wouldn't this mean a kind of self-incrimination at the end of the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I'll answer the two questions. The first question I believe was: Can someone be convicted for failing to prevent and failing to punish the same crimes by subordinates? Our position is, yes, provided the second and third elements -- or all three elements of superior responsibility are met. The person is a superior of the subordinates who commit the crime; when the crimes were committed, he had reason to know or knowledge that the crimes were about to be committed and did nothing to prevent them; if the crimes are, in fact, committed and the superior does nothing to prevent them, then he can be convicted -- or to punish them, I'm sorry, he can be convicted for punishing as well. That is not double jeopardy because it arises from a different a duty. One is a duty to prevent a crime from occurring, the other is a duty to punish it when it has occurred, and by punishing you're, therefore, discouraging them from committing other crimes or future crimes, and you're also discouraging your other soldiers from committing similar crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, but I want to insist on this. You're absolutely right what you say about the rationale behind the failure to punish, but isn't it true that starting attempts to punish -- of course, he can't himself punish, but he can address other organs able to prosecute, to do the necessary. But wouldn't it at the same time be necessary that Mr. Halilovic would have to admit that he omitted in the beginning to prevent the crime, thus it would amount to self-incrimination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: He doesn't admit anything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kremer, sorry for interrupting. Before I let you answer Judge Schomburg's last question, one point of clarification about the time used in this hearing. The Prosecution started five minutes later than they were supposed to start. So I would propose to let you go on until 4.00 p.m., instead of five to 4.00. Therefore, we could have a shorter break, a break going from 4.00 to 4.15 p.m., we would then resume at the time of 4.15. You may proceed. You may proceed until 4.15 -- no, sorry, until 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I wonder, Judge Schomburg, if you might be so kind as to repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yeah. My question was: Wouldn't it amount to self-incrimination if Mr. Halilovic would be obliged to report to the competent authorities that they should prosecute those events he himself was involved in -- by omitting to prevent the crime, thus amounting, as I said, to a certain extent to a self-incrimination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: The question, I think, makes an assumption that the individual commander or superior had actual knowledge that the crimes were about to be committed and did nothing to prevent them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: It may well be that in those circumstances the commander, depending on all of the circumstances, of course, may well be aiding and abetting the commission of the crimes by not intervening in light of the active knowledge, but that would require other circumstances, for example, whether he had in the past looked the other way at crimes committed by the subordinates, whether his failure to punish would be double jeopardy, our answer is, I think -- the case law recognised that -- that it is a superior can be convicted for both failing to prevent and punish the same set of crimes. Failure to prevent and failure to punish are different crimes committed at different times. I think I was saying that in answer to your question. Blaskic appeals judgement at paragraph 83: "Furthermore, the duty to prevent and the duty to punish are cumulative obligations. A superior is not at liberty to comply with one but not the other," that was found in four trial judgements Limaj 527, Halilovic, paragraph 72, Strugar, paragraph 373, and also paragraph 332 -- I'm sorry, that's three judgements. And the Strugar Trial Chamber convicted the accused in that case for failing to prevent and for failing to punish the unlawful shelling of the old town of Dubrovnik that happened at paragraph 446. And similarly the Hadzihasanovic Trial Chamber convicted the accused Kubura for failing to prevent and for failing to punish the plunder in Vares, and that's paragraph 1979. So there is lower-court authority on the double conviction. I don't believe that the issue relating to double jeopardy has been raised and I -- from my knowledge of at least the Hadzihasanovic case, I don't believe it's raised there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. To be abundantly clear, it's not a question of double jeopardy here; it's a question in concreto of maybe self-incrimination. And I think we have seen in the past that in the beginning of this Tribunal persons have been convicted for both liability under 7(1) and 7(3), but later on the jurisprudence developed that only a person can be held responsible under 7(1). And I think we are in a similar situation, only to submit to you this proposition. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I may have a better answer after the break, but my understanding of self-incrimination was always that it was a personal admission and more a matter for court than for action. But I'll try to get you a better answer before I conclude my remarks. I think it might be time for ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes, I have a clarification for Judge Vaz's questions about Dzankovic's follow-up. I'd refer you to paragraph 671 and also in paragraph 746. I can advise the Court that I'm more than two-thirds of the way through my submission, so I would expect that we will finish well on time today. I -- in other words, I'll be using less time than allotted, subject to questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: President, President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. President, just for our clarification, Mr. Kremer, would you tell us where you are exactly now on subgrounds of ground one? I'm asking because I had the impression that you indicated that you will be covering --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I will be covering the subgrounds relating to the other two elements. I'm -- I'm basically in 1(C), the error in fact in reaching the unreasonable conclusion, giving you the facts, assuming that you will find in our favour in respect of the first question on superior responsibility, that is the effective control issue. And by doing so, I am also illustrating how the evidence establishes effective control. So I've sort of blended the grounds for the purposes of this argument. Our brief is comprehensive on all of the issues, and I thought that it might benefit from a consolidation because the -- the ground of failure to punish sort of got lost in the course of the writing in various sections. So I've tried to, I hope, assemble it in a way that is -- is clear from the point of view of capturing the main points that we wish to raise, and also giving you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kremer, time has come for us to break until 15 past 4.00, 4.15. Then you will have an additional 45 minutes to complete your submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Kremer, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. In answer to Judge Schomburg's question, which I apologise to not having an answer to before the break, our position is the fact that you can be convicted of both failure to prevent -- to prevent and failure to punish does not breach your right against self-incrimination. Because in being required to initiate an investigation, you are not compelled to incriminate yourself as to having failed to prevent the crimes; you are just required to report the fact of the perpetration of the crimes and not your role in failing to prevent it. The obligation is focused on the reporting of the perpetrators and the crimes, with a view to their punishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I just -- in wrapping up the section on Halilovic's exercise or material ability to initiate measures, I'd like to refer to the team report again, Exhibit 130, to point out that the team report does, in fact, recommend criminal investigations and proceedings against various members of the ABiH as well as other measures, and point out as well that Halilovic did not exercise his authority as inspection team leader to make recommendations for criminal investigations and proceedings about the events in Grabovica. I'd like to move on now to Delic's statements which confirm, in our submissions, that Halilovic had effective control over the troops. And this is confirmed by Delic through orders or statements. There are many examples in the trial judgement where Delic invests Halilovic with authority and power and where Delic confirms this authority and power. The Delic 30 August order invests Halilovic with authority and power to head an inspection team, created specially to coordinate and conduct a multi-corps combat operation. The Trial Chamber in paragraphs 363, 367, and 369 finds that pursuant to the August 30 order and subsequent orders, Halilovic re-organised and resubordinated the units of the ABiH, was tasked with coordinating combat functions, and was tasked with reviewing combat-readiness and coordinating combat operations. Instead of finding that these inspection team leader functions and their subsequent implementation were clear indicators of effective control, the Trial Chamber found limitations on Halilovic's authority to issue orders in two ways: Drastic proposals required consultation with Delic and orders had to be kept -- had to be in keeping with his authority. When reviewing these limitations, the Trial Chamber did not cite evidence that Halilovic had ever proposed drastic measures requiring consultation with Delic; and if it occurred -- and did Halilovic's orders exceed his actual or implied authority, as described; and if so, when. Instead, the Trial Chamber looked at the words of the order as limitations on command of combat operations and failed to look at the evidence of the exercise of the inspection team leader functions in the context of the operation. The Delic order should not have been examined with only command of combat operations in mind. As mentioned earlier, effective control is measured by what an order says and if and how it is implemented. At paragraph 369 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber failed to appreciate that these two so-called limitations did not diminish the power and the authority Halilovic had over the troops, and it was his orders and actions that should inform the decision on his effective control of the perpetrators. A careful analysis of the trial judgement shows that that was why the Trial Chamber lost its way. The power and authority of Halilovic as inspection team leader is confirmed multiple times by Delic. There are several examples illustrating that Delic intended to place Halilovic in charge, in command, and in control of the operation. Halilovic complains to Gusic -- or complains that Gusic, the 6th Corps commander, is avoiding him, and Delic sends him an order to communicate with Halilovic, Exhibits 132 and 133. As mentioned earlier, Karavelic spoke to Delic about following a Halilovic order and Delic confirmed that he should subordinate his troops for the purposes after the operation. Delic told Alispahic, the ministry of the interior, that Halilovic personally would be in charge of the operation, having every opportunity to mobilise the supplies and equipment as well as the units needed to successfully run the combat activities, judgement 183. At paragraph 285, Delic told the chief of staff of the 6th Corps that Halilovic was in charge of the operation. Delic also confirms Halilovic's material ability to prevent and punish. On the 12th of September, Delic issued an order to Halilovic personally, Exhibit 157, referred to at trial judgement paragraph 307, in which he confirms Halilovic had effective control over the subordinates, the 1st Corps 9th Mountain Brigade, the perpetrators of seven of the murders in Grabovica, and that Halilovic had the material ability to prevent and punish. He even sets out the reasonable and necessary measures that should be considered in the circumstances to prevent future crimes and to punish these perpetrators. The order confirms that Halilovic has the material and ability to investigate. He's directed to check the accuracy of the information regarding the genocide. The order confirms that Halilovic has the material ability to punish. It says, if accurate: Isolate perpetrators and take energetic measures. Halilovic has the material ability to prevent future crimes, do everything to prevent such actions and order deputy commander of the 9th, Delalic, to return to Sarajevo in order to solve problems in unit. Halilovic had the material ability to take reasonable measures to prevent and punish. He was ordered to inform Delic about the measures taken. And the particular significance of this order is that it is specific -- it specifically identifies the 9th Brigade, the perpetrators of seven of the 13 murders. Concluding on the first element of superior responsibility, the trial judgement and the evidence proved that Halilovic had effective control. His effective control lay in his exercise of material abilities to take all measures associated with the planned combat operation, including resubordinating troops, billeting troops, planning combat operations, issuing strategic decisions, ordering troops into battle, and when he issued orders his orders were obeyed. This demonstrates that his orders to prevent or punish crimes would similarly be obeyed by subordinates. He had the material abilities to initiate an investigation, to resubordinate or transfer offenders out of the area, to isolate perpetrators, to follow through the investigation, and so on. He had the material ability to prevent and punish. In answer to question 2 by the Chamber, the answer is obviously yes. Halilovic's role as inspection team leader is an indicator of effective control, as I have just demonstrated. Had the Trial Chamber considered this evidence applying the correct legal standard, looking for effective control instead of command over combat operations, the Trial Chamber would have reached the only conclusion available on the evidence, and that is on the 8th and 9th of September, 1993, Halilovic was the superior of subordinates who committed the massacre in Grabovica. This takes me to the second and third elements of superior responsibility failure to prevent. The other two elements are a reason to know or knowledge of the crimes at the time to require him to prevent or punish and taking necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish. And I will address both elements in relation to first the failure to prevent and the failure to punish. In respect of the failure to prevent, before the crimes in Grabovica occurred Halilovic had reason to know that members of the 9th Brigade could murder civilians, and the Trial Chamber reviewed but did not make any findings on the evidence relating to the 9th Brigade's past criminal behaviour and the real and reasonable risk that they would commit crimes in Grabovica. This is ground two and is fully briefed in 3.1 to 3.28, and there is a question directed to Mr. Halilovic's counsel on this point, and I'll reserve my discussions on this point for the purpose of saving some time until our reply to what counsel opposite have to say. I'll focus now on failure to punish. The second element for failure to punish the crimes is proven by the finding that Halilovic knew on September 9th, shortly after the killings at Grabovica, that soldiers of the ABiH, including the 9th Brigade, were involved. Halilovic also had material ability to punish the perpetrators for the crimes in Grabovica. The evidence demonstrates that he did not take reasonable and necessary measures to punish them. While he did order Dzankovic to collect information on September 9th, after this order Dzankovic received no assistance from the inspection team because the inspection team left to go to the operation zone for reconnaissance and to plan the operation, paragraph 671. Moreover, the event was being kept secret to enable the success of the combat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kremer --

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Judge Shahabuddeen has a question to put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kremer, do correct me in case I'm wrong, but my impression is that before the break you had told this Chamber that Mr. Halilovic, in establishing the inspection team, had directed that team to forward its report to the command, I don't have your words now, but not to himself. Did that look to you as if Mr. Halilovic expected that any criminal sanctions were not to be applied by him personally?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: The statement according to Dzankovic was: Send the report to Sarajevo command. Dzankovic was part of the security -- Main Staff security administration. He would have reported to his direct superior, and in fact his report of September 13th and the subsequent report -- he only sent -- three reports all went to the Main Staff security command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Does that suggest that the thinking of the -- those who were in charge was that any criminal sanctions would be applied by the Sarajevo command and not by Mr. Halilovic himself?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Aside from this statement, Your Honour, I don't believe that there is any evidence to show what Mr. Halilovic himself was thinking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, you accept, do you, that those reports were not submitted to Mr. Halilovic himself?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes. But I would also comment on the fact that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kremer, Judge Meron has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kremer, to follow on the point made by my distinguished colleague, Judge Shahabuddeen. The material ability to punish, is it a necessary ingredient of control role? It can be done surely by, say, military police or a judge advocate general which has nothing to do with control of operations. It can be a command function, but is it necessarily a command function or a control function?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: The material ability to initiate proceedings may be limited to simply reporting the crimes to the appropriate authority from which you have reason to know that the authorities will investigate and prosecute if there is sufficient evidence. In this particular case, Dzankovic was told only to collect information and report it to Sarajevo command. The -- the case law suggests that one has to take effective steps, and our submission is that there were other steps that could have been taken, other measures, reasonable, necessary ones that Halilovic could and should have taken that resulted in his violation. It was simply not enough in this case to say to Dzankovic: Collect the information and report to Sarajevo command and then wash your hands of it. He had a higher obligation. He had an obligation to do more, and I'll get into that in a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kremer. My point was rather that you have spoken at some length about -- about the material ability to punish, and my point was that while material ability to punish may be related to effective control or command role, it can also be quite in independent of that role, for example, by judge advocate general or the military police. So the conclusions we can draw from that will be fairly limited. Because of the way you proceed with your argument, and I would like to perhaps help you with regard to the remaining argument that you are going to make by asking you now specifically a question with regard to subgrounds two, three, and four of the first ground of appeal, and you might find it useful to refer to that. It would help me if you were to explain specifically how if you prevailed on your arguments on subground two, three, or four of the first ground, this would require us to conclude that the Trial Chamber erred in not finding Halilovic to be the commander of the operation beyond a reasonable doubt. And we are still left to remind you, Mr. Kremer, with some -- at least I am, with some lack of comfort, shall we say, regarding the question whether or not in the trial court the Prosecution did not, pretty excusably, focus on effective control based on command. I realise that you referred to the indictment, to the pre-trial brief, and to the concluding brief, but wasn't in reference to the things that you would like to draw our attention to a sort of fairly marginal in relation to the heart of the argument that you make in the trial court, and of which Mr. Halilovic could have proper notice. You don't have to answer these points now, but if you could somehow integrate them in your argument, that would be useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: We've made a note of your question, Your Honour, and if you would permit, rather than take the time today, I'll use some of our time tomorrow to hopefully address those questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: If the President is agreeable, it's agreeable to me, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given that Judge Meron was kind enough to hear this tomorrow, I would like to say that Judge Shahabuddeen has a question to put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kremer, you have submitted that Mr. Halilovic's obligation was not merely to direct Dzankovic to submit his report to the Sarajevo command but that he had a higher obligation. I'm not clear as to what you base that proposition on. What occurs to me is this, there's an army in the field and there's a system in force, and does not a commander discharge his responsibilities to ensure that the troops under him carry out their functions in a becoming manner by triggering the sanctioning mechanism. The sanctioning mechanism would be this, that he would direct Dzankovic to investigate and submit a report to the Sarajevo command, for them obviously to do what is necessary. Is there anything to show that he had to do more? Is that not enough in a way, in a material way, to show that Mr. Halilovic did discharge his responsibilities by triggering the sanctioning mechanism?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Our submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say something along the same lines and put a question to you like that. You can answer both questions at the same time. So the question I have is the following: Is the Prosecution able to tell us whether the inspection which was conducted by Mr. Halilovic, how did this unfold? What prerogatives did he have? It is quite common that somebody in charge of an inspection should lead an investigation and hand this over to some other person who has the authority to conduct it. So I wanted to know what his functions were in the matter and how he was supposed to conduct this investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I think I was coming to the answer to both your question, Judge Vaz, and Judge Meron's question. And perhaps I can move there right now. It's our submission that the duty to punish requires the superior to conduct an effective investigation and to take active steps to ensure that the perpetrators will be brought to justice. The Trial Chamber recognised that in its judgement at paragraph 98 as being the applicable law. The test for whether asking Dzankovic to collect information and keep the Sarajevo command informed is insufficient, firstly because Halilovic did not ask that he be informed at paragraph 746, that is the finding. At 746 there is also a finding by the Trial Chamber that the evidence shows that at this point in time investigations were already under way. The evidence does not show that Sefer Halilovic initiated the investigations or that investigations were in any way carried through -- carried forward through his actions. So based on the findings of the Trial Chamber, Halilovic did not initiate investigations.
