There is evidence, and a substantial amount of evidence, that -- to the contrary in terms of initiating investigations or assisting investigations. The IKM inspection team actually directed that investigations stop. And if I could just refer you to trial judgement 684 and Exhibit 119. Dzankovic as well in trial judgement 688 and Exhibit 215 asked for assistance in respect of furthering his inquiry or investigation, if it can be called that, and he received no assistance, no assistance from the inspection team and no assistance from anyone else. Halilovic could have followed up with Dzankovic, the only person Halilovic had ordered to take any action, but he did not. Halilovic received the order from Delic, as I've commented on earlier, of 12 September, and this confirms, at least in Delic's mind, which he put to paper two days before the operation was to commence, in light of his familiarity with the battle plans and the situation on the ground at the time, affirming both that Halilovic is the superior, but more importantly that measures should be taken. If Halilovic, who did nothing in response to that order, had taken any steps, the situation would have been much different and perhaps the perpetrators of the crime may have been prosecuted. If he had checked the accuracy of the information that was given to him about the murders in Grabovica, it could have been determined that the crime scene was insecure and that bodies were removed, burned, and buried, and corrective steps could have been taken, but they weren't because Halilovic did nothing. That's in trial judgement 413, 414, 427, 482, 524, and 665. Investigations which were suspended on the order of the IKM and Sefer Halilovic, investigations started by the 6th Corps military command could have been restarted. There's evidence of that in trial judgement 684 and Exhibit 119. Halilovic was told to isolate the perpetrators and take energetic measures. If this measure had been taken, Halilovic could have arrested the perpetrators instead of using them for reconnaissance operations the next day and in combat operations until they returned to Sarajevo on the 20th of September. Third, he could have -- he was ordered -- ordered Delic to return to Sarajevo and Halilovic issued this order. Delalic could have been interviewed by the Main Staff security administration investigators. Delalic even threatened to return to Sarajevo and Halilovic was summoned to intervene to order Delalic and the 9th to remain for combat operations. He was asked to inform Delic about measures taken, and this I think answers, along with the previous references, Judge Meron's question. Had Halilovic wanted to inform Delic in his September 20th inspection team report, he could have mentioned the Grabovica crimes and he could have recommended measures against the perpetrators and their commander, Delalic. He could have recommended that criminal investigations be commenced, he could have recommended a forensic examination be commenced, he could have recommended any number of things that could have set in motion the necessary and reasonable measures to ensure that the perpetrators who were his subordinates at the time were properly investigated and properly punished. But instead what Sefer Halilovic did is he failed to take any reasonable and necessary measure to punish in these circumstances. He did one thing: He asked Dzankovic to collect some information and tell Sarajevo about it, not him. Let me conclude by submitting that the Trial Chamber applied the wrong legal standard to determine effective control, resulting in a finding that Halilovic was not the superior of soldiers who committed the Grabovica murders. It then suspended consideration of the other two elements of superior responsibility under Article 7(3) of the Statute. The application of the wrong legal standard was a fundamental error which caused the Trial Chamber to acquit Halilovic. And we respectfully request this Chamber to intervene to reverse this error. As our briefs and submissions demonstrate, there was substantial evidence before the Trial Chamber which is summarized in the trial judgement and the briefs to conclude beyond a reasonable doubt that Halilovic was the superior of the soldiers who committed the murders in Grabovica and that he had knowledge of them and failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent and punish the perpetrators. The Prosecution submits that the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt supports convictions for -- of Halilovic for murder as a war crime, based on his failure as a superior, under Article 7(3) to prevent the Grabovica murders committed by his subordinates, soldiers of the 9th Brigade; and failure to punish the Grabovica murders committed by his subordinates, ABiH soldiers, including seven murders committed by the 9th Brigade. The Prosecution has requested this Chamber to reverse the acquittal, to convict Mr. Halilovic for the 13 murders based on his Article 7(3) liability as a superior of the perpetrators. The Prosecution also requests the Chamber to impose an appropriate sentence. Ms. Baig will answer your question 7 in a few minutes, and I would, subject to questions, turn the floor over to Mr. Buck, who will briefly discuss ground 3, general and specific measures. I'm not sure how much time we have left, but I think we can finish in 15 minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have ten minutes left. [Trial Chamber and legal officer confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By conferring with my -- after conferring with my colleagues, we decided to give you an extra ten minutes, so you have 20 minutes in all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BUCK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, that's appreciated. Your Honours, I will address the third ground of appeal, which concerns the Trial Chamber's categorisation of the duty to prevent crimes into general and specific obligations. The issue arises because the Trial Chamber, for the first time, separated measures to prevent crimes into categories it labelled as general and specific, and appears to state that as a matter of law no liability can attach for a breach of a general obligation. Trial judgement at paragraph 80 states, I'll quote briefly: "The duty to prevent may be seen to include both a 'general obligation' and a 'specific obligation' to prevent crimes ... The Trial Chamber notes, however, that only the 'specific obligation' to prevent triggers criminal responsibility as provided for in Article 7(3) of the Statute." General measures, in the Trial Chamber's estimation, consist of prior preventive measures such as instructing troops on international humanitarian law. This rule sets up categories where they are not needed and eliminates consideration of relevant, probative, and admissible evidence. I will address briefly three points concerning this error and they problems it has created, these are that the new rule contradicts existing law; second, it negatively affects the law, not only on necessary and reasonable measures, but also on the notice requirement; and third, it creates a rigid rule which excludes relevant evidence. On the first point, this new categorisation and exclusion of liability is contrary to existing law. The Appeals Chamber has stated that what constitutes necessary and reasonable measures is not a matter of substantive law but of evidence, to be determined on a case-by-case basis. I refer you to the Blaskic appeals judgement at paragraph 72, and in fact that was quoted in the Halilovic trial judgement at paragraph 74. In other words, the trier of fact evaluates and duly weighs all the evidence without the distraction of labels and categories. However, this new rule creates categories of evidence, takes one category, and removes it from the Trial Chamber's consideration. In relation to this case, Halilovic knew of the 9th Brigade members' prior violent criminal behaviour. An obvious, necessary, and reasonable measure was to instruct those troops in their duties under IHL, particularly their duty not to harm civilians. This was addressed, Your Honours, at the Prosecution pre-trial brief, paragraph 180, and the Prosecution final trial brief at paragraphs 258 to 60, 274 to 276. Under existing law, as set forth by the Appeals Chamber, evidence of this failure to take measures would be considered along with other evidence. Under the new general measures rule, it would not. Evidence which is relative, relevant, and probative should be limited only by the words of Article 7(3), which says nothing about general and specific measures. This concludes my first point, except to mention that since this case was briefed, two trial judgements have discussed the general-specific distinction and have taken divergent views. These are the Hadzihasanovic and Kubura judgement and the Oric judgement. The Hadzihasanovic and Kubura trial judgement used the general-specific terminology, but included general measures in its consideration and even in its finding of superior responsibility in relation to the El Mujahedin crimes. I refer you to paragraphs 145 to 155 and paragraphs 1477 to 1484. The Oric judgement, however, appears to say that a superior's failure to fulfill general obligations does not entail superior responsibility per se. That's at paragraphs 327 to 331. And the Prosecution -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, I feel nudged by the clock. My apologies. The Prosecution has appealed the Oric finding ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have just been told that you're going extremely fast. Kindly slow down, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BUCK
utterances.text: May I recommence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may resume now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BUCK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and my apologies. The Oric trial judgement has been appealed by the Prosecution as a matter of general importance. The second point I wish to make is that this rule could affect the Chamber's analysis of the element of notice, that is, knowledge or reason to know that crimes have been committed. Proof of notice, like necessary and reasonable measures, is a matter of evidence considered on a case-by-case basis, Krnojelac appeal judgement, paragraph 156. If evidence of general preventative measures is excluded from the inquiry of whether necessary and reasonable measures were taken, then by extension that same evidence could be excluded from consideration of whether a superior had notice crimes would be committed. Let me explain. Crimes are more likely to be committed by troops unschooled in IHL and the rules of armed conflict. Therefore, a superior's knowledge that troops are unschooled in IHL is evidence of notice to him that a risk of crimes would be committed. The ICRC commentary to Article 86 of the Additional Protocol I makes this exact point. The Appeals Chamber in Celebici at paragraph 238 endorsed the ICRC commentary on this point, stating that, I paraphrase: The level and training and instruction of subordinate officers and their troops is general knowledge which could put a superior on notice of possible unlawful acts by his subordinates. In other words, applicable here, the Appeals Chamber has stated that failure to take what the Trial Chamber calls general preventative measures can be evidence that a superior is on notice of the risk that crimes will be committed. If the Trial Chamber's rule is adopted not to consider general measures under necessary and reasonable element, there is a risk that this rule will negatively affect the notice element as well. It would be inconsistent for the category of general preventative measures to be considered for the notice element and not considered for the necessary and reasonable measures element. My third point, Your Honours, the trial judgement at paragraph 88 states in relevant part: "It is evident that no criminal liability may attach to the commander for failure in this duty per se ..." This statement and the earlier quoted paragraph 80, set up a rigid rule. Rigid rules can lead to problems. For example, if the only necessary and reasonable preventative measure available is to train troops in IHL and behaviour toward civilians, and the superior failed to do so, no criminal liability could attach, even if in the circumstances of that particular case those measures could have prevented or impeded crimes. This example reinforces the wisdom of the existing law permitting the Trial Chamber to weigh all the evidence on a case-by-case basis. Your Honour, unless -- I have concluded. I welcome your questions, or I will turn the floor over to Ms. Baig.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Madam Baig, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. In question 7 you asked the Prosecution to identify relevant sentencing factors. The most important sentencing factor is the gravity of the crimes. Gravity requires a consideration of the particular circumstances of the case, as well as the form and degree of the participation of the accused in the crime. Mr. Halilovic's sentence must reflect his criminal responsibility for failing to prevent and punish the massacre of 13 civilians in the village of Grabovica. The first step in assessing gravity is to look at the crime itself. The crime here is murder. Two recent trial judgements, the Naser Oric case and the Hadzihasanovic case, have suggested that 7(3) responsibility creates a separate crime of dereliction of duty, a crime which is less grave which results in a lower sentence. The Prosecution has appealed these cases, arguing that this analysis and the lower sentence do not reflect the true gravity of the crimes. If this issue arises in your deliberations, the Prosecution would ask for the opportunity to file a brief in this case as well. In short, the dereliction of duty analysis stands in stark contrast to the overwhelming authority of jurisprudence from this Tribunal and the ICTR. In all previous cases, successful Article 7(3) prosecutions have resulted in convictions of the superior for the underlying crimes of the subordinates. The Appeals Chamber has repeatedly confirmed this correct approach, that Article 3 is a form of -- sorry, Article 7(3) is a form of participation in the crime in cases such as Blaskic, Delalic, Aleksovski, Naletilic, and Krnojelac. The Appeals Chamber has upheld convictions of superiors for the underlying crimes of the subordinates. The consistent approach of the jurisprudence is also reflected in the Appeals Chamber confirmation that an accused cannot be held concurrently -- cannot be concurrently convicted, both under Article 7(1) and Article 7(3) for the same conduct. Further support can be found in the plain wording of the Statute and in customary international law. Turning to the gravity of the murders themselves, Halilovic is responsible for failing to prevent seven murders committed by the 9th Brigade and for failing to punish these subordinates after the crimes were committed. He's also responsible for failing to punish six further murders committed in Grabovica by other ABiH subordinates. Murder is universally considered to be a very grave offence. In this case there are three additional aspects to this gravity which deserve note. First, Halilovic's sentence should reflect the vulnerability of the victims, civilians, many elderly, some invalid, many killed in their homes. A young girl was killed in her mother's arms. The sentence should also reflect the callousness of the killings, paragraphs 441 and 464 of the judgement note this. Finally, the sentence should also reflect the high rank of the accused, deputy commander, Chief of Staff of the ABiH, Halilovic was second in command of the whole army. He was leader of the expert inspection team sent to the area by the supreme commander to coordinate the combat operations. His senior position adds to the gravity of the crime. The Prosecution does not advance any aggravating factors. Turning to mitigating factors. In his final trial brief, Halilovic pleaded nine mitigating circumstances, five of these are appropriate considerations, but they deserve only minimum weight in light of the gravity of the crimes. These are: Halilovic's prior character, efforts to promote a multi-ethnic state, personal circumstances, personal conduct at trial, and voluntary surrender. The remaining four factors advanced by the Defence should not be considered mitigating. First, the Defence argued that the Trial Chamber should take into account as a mitigating factor the difficulty and pressure under which Mr. Halilovic was working at the time. According to the Blaskic appeal judgement and the Bralo appeal judgement, this is not a mitigating circumstance. Second, Halilovic argued at trial that cooperation of Defence counsel should be considered in mitigation of his sentence. The Krnojelac appeals judgement rejects this proposition. The third and fourth factors raised by Halilovic at trial suffer from the same defect, they are both inconsistent with a conviction. Halilovic argued at trial that he should be given mitigation for his efforts to bring law and order in the Bosnian army and his efforts to uncover the truth of the events and to punish the perpetrators. Both of these propositions are factually inconsistent with a conviction. In light of the gravity of the offence, the Prosecution maintains its trial recommendation of ten years' imprisonment. This is not affected by Halilovic's acquittal for the crimes committed in Uzdol or his acquittal for the further Grabovica murders that were pleaded at trial. Sentencing for those related crimes would have been concurrent. The murder of 13 civilians requires a minimum sentence of ten years in order to achieve the sentencing goals set out in the Blaskic appeals judgement. Superior responsibility, and I'm reaching my conclusion. Superior responsibility is the key means of preventing violations of international humanitarian law. A lenient sentence for superior responsibility fails to deter the conduct for which Halilovic should be convicted. Wilful disregard of his legal obligations to protect civilians through his powers to prevent or punish. Halilovic should be convicted of the Grabovica massacre, and he should be sentenced to ten years' imprisonment. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Judge Meron has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Ms. Baig, how do you suggest I should read or what conclusions I should draw from this statement in paragraph 746 of the trial judgement: "The Trial Chamber finds that based on the evidence it cannot be concluded that Sefer Halilovic had the material ability to punish the perpetrators of the crimes committed in Grabovica"?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Justice Meron, this particular sentence forms part of the Prosecution's appeal. In the appeals brief you will see that we argue that this is an error of logic. In this instance they take the fact that Sefer Halilovic did nothing in terms of necessary -- in terms of taking the necessary and reasonable measures that he could have taken, and they use that to conclude that on the first element that he had no material ability to do so. This is illogical. The proper approach would have been to consider whether he had the material abilities to prevent, punish, or initiate measures leading to proceedings, as required by the Blaskic appeals judgement, to look for the indicia of effective control. And from that indicia that shows the hierarchical relationship then move to the other elements, and here they flipped it on its head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Shahabuddeen has a question now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Baig, I want to express my gratitude to you for a very clear presentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: But tell me one thing. I recall your submission to the effect that convictions cannot be made under Article 7, paragraph 1, and Article 7, paragraph 3. Now, if I'm right in recalling your submissions, this question comes to mind: Is it that convictions cannot be made under both paragraphs or that convictions should not be made under both paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Justice Shahabuddeen, my understanding of the case law of the Appeals Chamber is that when faced with facts, the same conduct which shows both a 7(1) and a 7(3) form of participation, the Trial Chamber should begin with the 7(1) analysis and then use the superior position of the accused as an aggravating factor in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So you -- your perception of the matter is that double convictions cannot be made?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Justice Shahabuddeen, that is my understanding of the case law --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: -- I think that the purpose is to ensure at sentencing that the full conduct of the accused is reflected but that double convictions aren't entered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I only wanted to know what was your position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: You have the floor for 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Let me repeat for the record. You have the floor for 45 minutes for your response.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court pleases. Your Honour, it's the Defence submission that this judgement did justice, that it did justice for the victims of the crime. The killers were identified, the story has been told, and the records been made. It's our submission too that justice was done to Mr. Halilovic, who was presumed innocent and ultimately was acquitted after a trial which finished within the relevant time and was concluded with a cautious and pain-staking judgement that expressed relevant views responding to the indictment and dealt with the major and important factual issues that arose. Your Honours, I'm going to move very quickly to ground one, sub one in the Prosecution's appeal brief, but I wish to make a preliminary comment before I do. The procedural checks that exist upon appellants in this Chamber are extremely significant ones in the unusual circumstances of an appeal against a full acquittal by the Prosecution. Those appeal standards protect Mr. Halilovic here. The standard which the Prosecution must meet when contesting the Trial Chamber's factual findings is a high one, as the Court well knows, and the Bagilishema appeals judgement at paragraph 14 provides that: "The Prosecution faces a more difficult task. It must show that when account is taken of the errors of fact committed by the Trial Chamber, all reasonable doubt of the accused's guilt has been eliminated." Your Honour, the practice on appeal of deference to the Trial Chamber is also an important matter which Mr. Halilovic calls in aid here, that deference is well-established, and I'll say no more about it. This trial -- this Chamber is not to be treated as a second Trial Chamber simply to re-run an argument. There are also limits on appellants which protect Mr. Halilovic, an acquitted accused, which far from being technicalities are important matters. The rules concerning waiver protects respondents and Trial Chambers from arguments which weren't put previously and likewise an effective way, they might be discerned if an argument was raised but raised obscurely in a way that the Trial Chamber and the Defence were not in a position of notice to deal with them properly. Variation of grounds without leave, the abandonment of grounds, and meeting the high burden of argument are matters which all appellants are subjects to, but it's very important on an appeal by an acquitted accused that they be enforced because an accused are, for many reasons, human rights reasons, resources reasons, are exposed to a level of hardship. This Tribunal does permit, of course, appeals against conviction. The very fact of that means that we are foreclosed from saying it's unfair. We don't make that submission, but we do say that the protections that exist in the appeal system are very important ones, and it's not artificial or wrongful to enforce them strictly, and we ask that that be done in this case. It is our submission that this is a safe and a mainstream acquittal, a predictable one. The judgement features constant, correct, articulations of the law and indeed as when we come to the question of effective control, it's conceded by the Prosecution that the articulations in the judgement at 57 to 63 are not to be impeached. What the Prosecution is saying is that a wrong lens was interposed between the facts and the correct articulation of the law that took place. There was also a careful and complete articulation of facts and we've -- what I characterise as trivial exceptions, the Prosecution do not take issue without the fact that the -- that the Trial Chamber looked at the relevant material. The Prosecution submit to you that this appeal is, and I quote: "About effective control," but it's really about the notice. It's about the notice that's before you and the grounds that are contained in it. That's what's at issue here. The Trial Chamber wrestled explicitly with the material facts that were pled in the indictment. The findings were responsive to that indictment. It's not available to the Prosecutor to contend here that simply because the Trial Chamber made factual findings, they must be in error, or that they elicitly focused on a de jure cusp. The Trial Chamber focused upon the material facts that were pleaded in the indictment and dealt with them appropriately and cannot be criticised for doing so. Your Honour, I'm about to turn to ground one, and throughout the Prosecutor's brief and in submissions here, it's become evident that the Prosecutor has sought to draw a distinction between command and effective control. In other words, the Prosecutor say that there's been a wrongful focus upon command by the Trial Chamber at the expense of a proper analysis of effective control. But, Your Honours, in a military situation such as this one was, the chain of command and military doctrines will always be important. It's not necessary that a Chamber artificially restricts its analysis to formal matters, and in fact in many cases that may produce error. That's not what happened here. It was no error to focus on those matters and in fact it was required of the Trial Chamber to do so. In this case, effective control was pleaded and pursued, and I quote from the indictment: "By virtue of Halilovic's status as the commander of Neretva 93." At paragraph 38 of the indictment, and forgive me for reading it but it's the indictment we hold strongly to in this appeal, the Prosecution pleaded: "At all times relevant to the charges in the indictment, by virtue of his position and authority as commander of the operation, he had effective control over the units subordinated to him. These included the 9th motorised Brigade, the 10th Mountain Brigade, the 2nd Independent Battalion, and the Prozor Independent Battalion." The Prozor Independent Battalion, Your Honours will recall, was the offending unit in the Uzdol branch of this matter. Now, nowhere else in the indictment did the Prosecution say by virtue of anything. The -- the -- Halilovic exercised effective control. Your Honours, I turn therefore to the first ground of appeal, and that concerns effective control. The Prosecution of course say that this is an effective control case. It's a little artificial, Your Honour, because in this Tribunal it was said by my learned friend, I don't have the page reference, but I'll provide it tomorrow, that this wasn't a de jure case at all. But the indictment makes it clear that it was and the paragraph -- foot -- 3 makes it clear that the Prosecution allegation was that Halilovic was appointed to command. It cannot be avoided, Your Honour. Just forgive me a moment, I apologise. I draw the Court's attention here to paragraphs 3 and 4 of the -- of the indictment and to those passages that I'm going to be taking you to from the Prosecution's pleadings and final arguments which I won't read out in total because they're in our brief, but some parts of it need to be stressed. Your Honours, as an introduction to that, in relation to liability under Article 7, sub-3, there's always a very important focus upon the nature of the relationship between the defendant and the perpetrators. And so, as it was expressed in a decision in the Krnojelac proceedings, a decision on the preliminary motion on the form -- I'm sorry, I'm going fast. A decision on the preliminary motion on the form of the amended indictment dated the 11th of the 2nd, 2000, at paragraph 18, what was said, among other things, is: "What is most material: A, the relationship between the accused and the others who did the acts." And, Your Honours, this indictment does provide notice of that. That was the way that the Prosecution put their case. The Prosecution, fulfilling their duty to be fair with the defendant and to allow both the Trial Chamber and the defendant and counsel for counsel for the Prosecution presenting the case to put the argument in a focused and intelligible way, put their case in that way in paragraph 38. Your Honours, it's not merely a formal matter that that was done, it was sensible and predictable. In this case Halilovic was a senior officer, and the killers were some of them as young as 17 years old, young soldiers without rank. There were many degrees of separation between Halilovic and these individuals, and therefore it was important for the Prosecution to plead as they always must a chain of command. They had to plead a chain of command here, and in a military setting it was inevitable that was so. And they did. In this case the chain of command was pleaded and clearly and articulately and explicitly pursued in this way. Halilovic was appointed to command the operation Neretva 93. It was commanded from the IKM at Jablanica and this is the Prosecution case, contrary to what was put by my learned friend. We say this is the way the case was put. It was commanded from the IKM at Jablanica, 9th Brigade soldiers were subordinated to it, and the Prozor Independent Battalion elsewhere was subordinated to it. The chain of command with respect to the killers at Grabovica went from Sefer Halilovic through Zulfikar Alispago and the Zuka unit, the Zulfikar unit, through Ramiz Delalic to the troops. In the course of the operation, some of these soldiers committed crimes Halilovic had the material ability to prevent and whilst they were still subject to him or subordinate to him to punish. It was by virtue of his position and authority as commander of Neretva 93 that Halilovic exercised effective control. The material facts listed elsewhere in the indictment under the heading superior responsibility demonstrate the reality of that effective control, his seniority, the orders he gave, and so on. Your Honours, at paragraph 111 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber found explicitly that this was the way the Prosecution put its case, and they made that explicit finding in terms at paragraph 111. And a perusal of the notice of appeal will reveal to you that that paragraph's not appealed. That paragraph's not mentioned in the notice of appeal. And when the Prosecution allege that it's always been their case, you may have doubt about that because they didn't appeal paragraph 111, and although they criticise it now, it didn't form part of the appeal. Your Honour Judge Meron asked a question of the Prosecutor earlier on as to where it might be said at trial that they advanced this case beyond command, and the learned Prosecutor replied to you that they are between paragraphs 142 and 186 of the final brief of the Prosecution that could be found. Well, it can't be, and a perusal of those paragraphs will not yield any such case, no matter how it's cut. Paragraph 186, the concluding one, is absolutely explicit. And, I make mention that in paragraph 111 of the judgement, that's cited. Paragraph 186 provides: "The Prosecution submits that the evidence adduced at trial has proved beyond a reasonable doubt that Halilovic planned, organised, commanded, coordinated, and inspected Operation Neretva. Halilovic had command authority over the units that participated in Operation Neretva. The evidence also established that this command authority was effective and that Halilovic's command was obeyed in practice. Therefore, he had effective control of the troops who participated in this military operation." There was no case beyond command. Your Honours, it was a rational and sensible way for the Prosecution to proceed. The fact that the facts weren't proved doesn't create an error of law; it just means that the evidence let the Prosecution down at trial. Your Honours, the findings of fact by the Trial Chamber can be found -- I won't canvass this because of time reasons, other than to point out that many findings of fact that the Trial Chamber made were in direct response to allegations of material facts in the indictment. Thus at paragraph 372 the Trial Chamber found he was not appointed and he was not the commander of Neretva 93. Paragraph 363, he was not appointed at the Zenica meeting. The Zenica meeting is an example of exactly what went wrong with the Prosecution case. This was a meeting where it was said that Halilovic had discussed, proposed, and argued for a particular operation. But the Defence was in a position to put to witnesses and to tender evidence material which just not only raised a doubt but proved beyond any shadow of a doubt the complete contrary. The matter simply wasn't discussed there. The Prosecution did have a case of de jure command and appointment, it just failed on the facts. Your Honours, what emerged from the evidence at trial was a rather different picture of Halilovic. It was a picture of Halilovic with a limited role with no de jure power, no de facto power, an uncertain limited level of influence, no chain of command in which he participated, and no power over the perpetrators, and no effective control over the perpetrators. The picture of Halilovic not being in the chain of command is important and Halilovic being unable to compel obedience in any meaningful way from the wrong-doers or those in the chain of command allegedly leading to him is instructed. An excellent example of that is the evidence relating to Zulfikar Alispago and the Zuka -- I'm sorry, that was his nickname, the Zulfikar unit. At the pages -- or paragraphs 744 and 745 of the judgement it's evident there that not only was the Zulfikar unit not resubordinated to Halilovic, but that Zulfikar Alispago was anything but obedient or complicit with him. And, Your Honours, it would not be to the point for the Prosecutor to say that they could find one or two or more occasions when Zulfikar Alispago cooperated with Halilovic. The point is this: Halilovic could not compel him, and it was evident and the Trial Chamber considered the realities of resubordination and that's why they mentioned that matter. One could design a chart and prove that Halilovic was or was not in a particular relation. The Trial Chamber didn't commit that error. They looked at the real evidence and the evidence concerning Zulfikar Alispago was anything but supportive for the Prosecutor. Alispago reported directly to Delic as was proved in the evidence. There was an exhibit 201, a rather irrelevant exhibit in many ways concerning helicopters, but it was a direct report from Alispago to Delic. The order which Alispago wrote to the troops under his control, it used to be called Exhibit 273, and could I apologise because throughout we've referred to it as Exhibit 273 only to find that later on it was transformed after being re-translated into Exhibit 503. But it's a combat order given by Zulfikar Alispago which does not acknowledge Halilovic or Neretva 93 or Neretva or an IKM and makes no reference to him at all. It would appear that that's an order he made after tearing up the proposal sent by the inspection team. The Defence brief at paragraphs 347 to 353 deals with that matter. Your Honour, although the Trial Chamber didn't go this far because they didn't need to, the Defence also pointed to -- sorry. Pardon me, Your Honours. The Defence also points to the matters raised in the Defence brief at paragraphs 340 to 346 and 358 to 375, if you need to revisit the facts on this matter a very good guide to the situation of Ramiz Delalic and his unit and the relations between that unit and Halilovic and the relations between that unit and Zulfikar Alispago is well set out. What we say is that those matters always raised a doubt. Even if Halilovic had been appointed de jure to command Neretva 93, the fact that he was unable to exact obedience from those individuals, particularly with respect to the power to prevent and punish would have stood like a line in the path of a conviction, but it's not necessary to do that. That was not the Prosecution's case, and it's our submission that their case exclusively proceeded by means of a chain of command. I quote from learned prosecuting counsel on the 30th of the 8th at page 60, 30th of August of 2005 at page 67, that was in the closing address, and when speaking of how Halilovic retained effective control over the relevant individuals at the relevant time, counsel said this: "And not for one moment did Mr. Halilovic lose his command and control over those units because Zuka was subordinate -- sorry, Zuka was subordinated to his inspection team -- Zuka's unit was subordinated to him and through Zuka the 9th and 10th Brigades were subordinate to Mr. Halilovic." The chain of command was explicit. Your Honour, turning to ground one, this ground is pleaded as -- as made up of six subgrounds and it stands or fall with the six subgrounds. We say it doesn't gain any strength as a subground at all as a collection of grounds. The Prosecution allege each ground singly or in combination or they have done until today. As I understand it, however, here there was a withdrawal with respect to one of those, either sub two or sub three in the sense that it could not singly justify the overturning of a finding of effective control. We'll look at the transcript and give an accurate account of that, but it is your submission that none of those subgrounds, alone or in combination, even if established, could suffice to overturn the finding of effective control, which ultimately was made in terms of effective control without any reference to any de jure or de facto command focus, without reference to any wrong lens. At paragraph 752 it is further found that Halilovic did not have effective control over those individuals. Your Honours, we do take issue generally speaking with the matters the Prosecution raises in its opening when dealing with this as a ground at large, we've done that in our brief, and I won't seek that delay about. You'll note that there's no -- we submit no argument from the Prosecution as to how the different combinations of grounds might play out. In other words, if this Tribunal upheld subgrounds 2 and 4 but not others, it places the Defence in a difficult position to respond to those. But what we submit is that on the face of it, subgrounds two and three could never reach the standard. Subgrounds four, five, and six do not try to reach the standard, and subground one, we say would find that even if established, even if established, because there was still open a reasonable doubt that Halilovic would exercise effective control over the killers because they were 9th Brigade troops, his control was supposed to go through Zulfikar Alispago, that chain is broken, and effectively not appealed and no argument has been directed to that or has been so far. Your Honours, we turn now to ground sub -- one sub one, and this we say in answer to Your Honours' question, the first of the questions, we say this has been abandoned and unequivocally so. In the notices an allegation that Trial Chamber failed to find that Halilovic was the de facto commander of an operation called Neretva 93. At that time, the time of the notice, the Prosecution appeal was consistent with the findings of the Trial Chamber at paragraph 111 that the case was about command. So the Trial Chamber found that it was about command at 111, the Prosecution didn't appeal that, conformed their appeal to that, and said that the error was that the Trial Chamber failed to find Halilovic was de facto commander. Your Honours, we pause to say this: We can't meet the various -- the variations in the time allotted. We would give no more than a trivial argument orally. So we refer to what we say in the brief about that. But I would point out this, that with respect to that allegation, the very text of the judgement rebuts it. The Trial Chamber explicitly and carefully explored issues of de jure and de facto command, repeatedly did so, did not restrict themselves to the de jure evidence military manuals and so on, but conceded what happened in the field and conceded the orders issued and what story those orders might have told about the authority of those issuing them and those standing behind them. The Prosecution, we submit, are mistaken in saying that is -- that there was an overfocus on the formalities. And paragraphs 372 and 752 we say are quite clear. The Trial Chamber was cautious, and we say no more than about it other than what's in the brief. The notice that's before this Court made some unsustainable claims in support of that proposition, therefore the second sentence alleges that the Trial Chamber required command as a necessary element of effective control, but they didn't do any such thing. Never did they require command as a necessary element of effective control as an abstract proposition of law. And this really is, in our submission, an endeavour to turn a sensible approach to the facts into an error of law. The Trial Chamber didn't articulate an error, so it's said to be implicit. The third sentence: "The Trial Chamber erred in concluding that a person tasked with coordinating combat activities could not, by virtue of that position, have effective control over the offending troops, but again that error was not made in terms. That is a version, an interpretation of what the Trial Chamber did, attempting to impute an error of law to what is just a plain finding of fact. Sentences four and five constitute the ultimate proposition that was raised. We say that's abandoned. Why do we do that because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey, could you please slow down. I'm not following the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours -- I've got prior convictions for this I'll endeavour to do my best, but I welcome any signs to slow down. Your Honours, was the notice abandoned -- sorry, was the argument of the notice abandoned? Well, the whole thrust of the argument that's now put, and it's explicitly put by my learned friend Mr. Kremer, here is that this case is all about effective control beyond command and that it was an error to focus on command. Now, paragraph 2.16 of the Prosecution argument in the brief may be read as an explicit abandonment of that proposition. What the Prosecution said the Trial Chamber had a duty to do was: They had a duty to continue with that inquiry and to determine whether he nonetheless had superior authority over the perpetrators because he was the most senior ABiH officer in the region or because he was the team leader of the inspection team. No mention there of because he was a de facto commander. So -- and I'd ask you to note in that regard, too, the way the argument has changed with respect to subgrounds two and three because in each case where as in the notice those grounds were dealt with as raising the danger that the Trial Chamber has wrongly acquitted Halilovic of being the de facto commander, that's not pressed anymore. And it's a pattern of ditching and dropping quietly the references to commander for something more neutral and vague, something approximating superior responsibility. Hence we have references to the most superior officer. It used to be the most senior commander, paragraph 36 of the indictment, it was the most senior commander. Your Honours, such references as there are to de facto command are sporadic. And although my learned friend now, and I say skillfully, constructs an argument that de facto command is just one of the small parts of effective control. It's inconsistent with the criticisms levelled at the Trial Chamber for its focus on command, and it's inconsistent with the argument that there was a case beyond command. Therefore, Your Honours, we say the answer to question number 1 is yes it's abandoned. And if it's not abandoned, then it is -- Your Honours ought not to not deal with it because it's inadequately argued and supported. It simply hasn't been dealt with and new argument has emerged. So if logical connections can be made to say that the argument is not abandoned, it's effectively abandoned. If not abandoned it's so likely argued, we submit, that this ground fails, and we refer to our brief for the substance of it. I turn now to the issue of what we say is the new appeal theory, the case beyond command. I've already dealt with this in some limited ways. This new argument of the Prosecutors has three elements to it. Would you excuse me, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. So that the Prosecution says that the first error consists in focusing on command; the second error consists in finding -- failure to make necessary findings regarding the case beyond command; and the third error, which is effectively a factual error, and that is failure to find Halilovic guilty or at least failure to find Halilovic was in fact the effective -- in effective control of those units. Now, we point this out, the first of those can be dealt with very shortly. It's not an error -- the focus on command was not an error. It was necessary. It would have been a complete error not to focus on command. That's the way the trial was run, it's the way the indictment was structured. We'd be here on a clear error of law if the Trial Chamber did not focus on command, and they had to do that. And nowadays, Your Honour, of course the Prosecution have finally and somewhat reluctantly come to admit that. In the reply brief, the Prosecution said well, and I quote: "The Prosecution primarily pursued command responsibility." You'll see that at 4.4. Now, there's an unease about the Prosecution's submissions here because today it's a little different. They're saying it was always about effective control, but it's really an argument in search of a theory. Your Honours, the second part of that argument, part (B) in their brief, refers to the error of law that the Trial Chamber failed to make necessary findings, and part (B)1 is that there was a case beyond command. Your Honours, should this part not be proved by the Prosecution, it has two effects: The first is that they may be taken to have waived this argument; the second is that as a matter of substance, even if you were not satisfied that they had waived the argument - and we urge that you should - they have alleged an error of law in not dealing with it; and we say and submit that it's no error of law to ignore this argument completely. We'll add as a third and final fail-safe that the findings of the Trial Chamber and the careful analysis of the evidence renders the whole point fruitless in any event because the Trial Chamber did look at de facto commander, and the rest of the argument is far-fetched in our submission. But the two issues I've phrased are important ones because the issue of waiver is one that justifies summary dismissal, but the Prosecution are alleging legal error and the burden falls, therefore, upon them to demonstrate that it was a legal error by the Trial Chamber. It's not for me, for the Defence, to establish in the circumstance of this case that it was waived, although we say we do establish that. It's for the Prosecution to show that there was an error. Now, Your Honours, I'll refer you to paragraphs 24 to 40 of our respondent's brief. I refer you to paragraph 38 of the indictment, as I already have. The Prosecution's pre-trial brief is referred to and discussed at paragraph 32 of our brief. This sounds uninteresting, but it may be useful for later reference. So the Prosecution's pre-trial brief is discussed in our brief at paragraph 32. Paragraph 33 of our brief refers to pre-trial motions and to later filings. Paragraph 35 and 36 of our brief refer to the Prosecution opening and the Prosecution final brief and a full quote from the Prosecution final brief at paragraph 186. I've read that to you already and I won't repeat it. The Prosecution, Your Honour, having put their case as clearly as they could, then met a finding by the Prosecution -- by the Trial Chamber at paragraph 111 that that had been done. Now, we submit that, number one, that's a clear waiver. There couldn't be a clearer waiver. They did not run this argument at trial and it's finished. However, if you weren't satisfied that it was a waiver, you would nevertheless not find that it was an error of law. This is the lens which the Prosecution claim to have proffered to the Trial Chamber, which the Trial Chamber failed to look through at the evidence. Now, this lens was not offered at all. But if, by cunning argument, the Prosecution can construct the way in which it was offered, it was offered so obscurely and so unclearly as to constitute no error of law, to ignore it altogether. And it would be an astounding situation, Your Honours, if on appeal the Prosecution could say the Trial Chamber missed it, the Defence missed it, and our own barristers missed it, but now you can convict. That would be an astounding position, and we submit that it cannot be so. Your Honours, the Prosecution's claims to the contrary are very contorted, but I'll say no more about it now because my learned friend drew Your Honours' attention to those pages in the closing brief, and they don't support the thesis that they allege that they would. So I'll move on now. Your Honours, appeals are not guessing games, and I think Your Honours have heard enough about that. I'll move on to something else. Thank you very much. Two effects, though, procedural and substantial. There is a waiver. It's very unfair to the accused. It places the accused in a terrible position at trial to face the case that's obviously focused upon real command responsibility, classical command responsibility, all of a sudden to be found that it's a vaguer and broader version of it. That's not how the Trial Chamber saw it or the Defence saw it and there's no error established. Your Honours, that should end the matter, but we're not here to climb onto a horse and say that we have the argument. In the event that it went further, the two matters that the Prosecution says should have been analysed were Halilovic's status as the most senior-ranking officer in Herzegovina and his leadership of the inspection team. The position as most senior-ranking officer of Herzegovina, Your Honour, we would say there's two ways in which we can deal with that. The first is that the Trial Chamber should not be likely found to have erred in this regard. They considered a massive evidence about it explicitly and took time over it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Morrissey, you have ten minutes to conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm grateful for the indication. The argument from the Prosecutors concerning the most senior-ranking officer in Herzegovina features an interesting terminological change from the notice. In the indictment at paragraph 36, this was the most senior commander. In the notice of appeal there is no reference to this new theory. In the appellant's brief, it emerges as most senior-ranking officer. There was no evidence about what it meant to be -- I submit no reliable evidence as to what it meant to be the most senior-ranking officer. All right. I draw the Court's attention to the Prosecution's continued reliance upon evidence which was criticised heavily by the Defence and was found by the Trial Chamber to be evidence from witnesses who required corroboration. Those witnesses were Ramiz Delalic, Salko Gusic, Bakir Alispahic, Nedzad Mehanovic, Witness D, and Erdin Arnautovic. In respect of each at paragraph 17, footnote 34 was a finding that these witnesses were not completely reliable. And what we submit is that it is not open to the Prosecution to attempt to revive a case based on their evidence or to invite the Chamber to act upon that evidence now without seeing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours -- so with respect to the most-senior officer argument, we say it was raised obliquely, it was raised as part of the command case, and the current version of it is not properly before this Chamber. But in any event the short answer to it is that Halilovic's senior status lent him influence only. There's an explicit finding by the Trial Chamber at 752 about this matter. The case law concerning influence has been referred to in our brief at paragraphs 101 to 103 and in the Defence final trial brief at paragraphs 189 to 195. And influence, even rising to a high level of being able to give orders or having some charisma, play an important role is not enough. And in this case, there's an explicit finding that deals with such influence as Halilovic was able to bring to bear, but his status as a senior commander was not a source for effective control, either inside or outside the argument that was conducted at trial. It has to be stressed that the Trial Chamber considered all relevant evidence - and this is discussed at paragraphs 64 to 66 of -- of the respondent's brief. The judgement at 747 made it clear explicitly that the Trial Chamber had considered all the evidence. Trial Chambers are not likely to be found to have ignored evidence or forgotten about evidence or overlooked evidence even when they don't mention it. In this case this is a very careful judgement. Furthermore, the evidence was that in fact Halilovic was treated with relevant -- relative disrespect. Apart from the material I've already referred you to, the evidence about Uzdol was persuasive and important. A witness was called, Witness J, who on the 7th of July, 2005, at page 98, was asked questions by the learned Trial Judge, Judge El Mahdi, concerning whether or not -- the translation was whether Halilovic has clout. Witness J was the -- was in the security administration of the Prozor Independent Battalion, that's Uzdol, that's not Grabovica. However, the very same command structure was alleged by the Crown -- by the Crown, I'm sorry, by the Prosecution with respect to Uzdol, as with respect to Grabovica. The evidence is clearly relevant in that regard. What Witness J is r said is: "My impression was he had no practical power at all." Now, that's not a de jure or unfocused or overly formal finding; that's direct evidence about the clout and abilities of Halilovic. Witness J is a witness who it was open to the Trial Chamber to fully believe, and the perusal of his evidence might lead this Chamber to the same conclusion if you needed to, if you needed to engage in that. Secondly, as to the most senior commander, there was no doctrinal evidence which supported any idea that a most-senior commander standing somehow outside the chain of command could have effective control. A question asked earlier on by His Honour, the Presiding Judge, raised this as an issue, and what we submit is that the military context of this -- of this case is of importance. The fact that Halilovic was not important does tell a military person something. Other military people will take a great interest in whether somebody has been appointed or not. The Trial Chamber and -- sorry, Trial Chambers generally, and this Chamber also in particularly, is not to be bound by local laws and local structures, but it doesn't mean that it's irrelevant, particularly in the case where Halilovic, a high and senior person, is said to be linked with young people who have committed crimes through a number of different degrees of separation. Doctrinal significance is very important. The Prosecution failure in de jure terms here is something we rely upon very, very strongly because it's not a neutral matter. The Prosecution cannot simply set aside the de jure evidence and say, Well, we failed on that but there still remains the possibility of de facto. It's the other way around. This is an army. The failure of the de jure case is very important, and the Trial Chamber was fully entitled to take into account and to enunciate as much or as little of this as they saw fit; that Halilovic's ability to effectively control people should be seen by this as explicitly conceded in this court today for the first time Halilovic was not appointed. Not just that it wasn't proved, he was not appointed. That's what the Prosecution has put here. That is a significant and relevant fact. Your Honours, even if the senior status wasn't taken account of, it would have no impact whatsoever on the findings of effective control and we urge you to set it aside. The next issue -- excuse me, please. Your Honours, I'll deal with -- I'll commence the issue of the inspection team leader. Here, once again, Your Honours, a belated construction, we submit, is evident. And Your Honours will look to the indictment to see whether or not under the heading of the -- of superior responsibility there was any reference to effective control by virtue of being the inspection team leader. There isn't. The only -- in the notice there is -- in the notice of appeal at 1, sub 1, there is a reference to a finding that a coordinator cannot, by virtue of that role, have effective control, but that's not sufficient. In any event, we point out that there are inadequacies in the light of this argument comes before the Court now as in part of the new case beyond command, but they probably subsumed any other criticism. As to the substance of this, we say it has no merit. The power Halilovic had as leader of the inspection team is similar in many ways to the power of a Chief of Staff. It put him beside the chain of command and not in it. It did not by any means give him power to command. It was -- as was said in the high command case as Chief of Staff: "He did not have authority in or with the chain of command and an order of his own signature would not have authority for subordinates in the chain of command." Now, the Trial Chamber had made a specific finding that they were not satisfied that he was Chief of Staff, so I use this argument by way of analogy rather than by saying that you're bound by any of the arguments that may be put on behalf of the Chief of Staff in a particular situation. But the Trial Chamber were safe in accepting that Halilovic's orders were not necessarily indicative of command power or of effective control at all. When my learned friend pointed you to Exhibit 161, that was an order given by Halilovic to certain troops, to Karavelic, to make a selection from certain troops to come down to Herzegovina. That was the order which Karavelic, the commander of the 1st Corps, did not obey. What he obeyed was the order of Commander Delic, to whom he turned, in an effort to -- to see what he had to do. And it was Delic and the force of Delic which compelled Karavelic to do what he was asked to do. Halilovic's own power did not suffice to have him obeyed. These are doctrinal matters that -- and they intersect in this case in a variety of ways, but the Trial Chamber was very alert to this issue and how the orders given by Halilovic might be used to interpret his powers. But it would be open to -- it was open to and of course naturally would have been open to the Trial Chamber to accept what was said by witnesses about this. One witness, for example, was the witness Vehbija Karic, who in Exhibit 444 gave a variety of comments about the powers that the inspection team had. And at page 102 of that exhibit, he made the comment, my note here is -- it's not very full, I'm sorry, but I'll refer the Court to page 102 where Karic commented that the commanders were aware that we didn't have a command function. I'll give you the proper quote tomorrow. This is a note of mine, I apologise, it's not verbatim so I have -- there's other comments at page 103 and 106 about these matters. Your Honours, this evidence was fully considered and findings were made in detail about it, paragraphs 103 -- I'm sorry, paragraphs of the judgement 193 to 205, paragraph 210 to 221 concern the IKM, and there were a variety of comments made, one by Jusuf Jusarevic a witness who described Namik Dzankovic as a free shooter, and he said about Dzankovic -- that was an -- I've now strayed into the area of military security at the end of the day but -- and I'll say more about this tomorrow, but as for Dzankovic, he being a military security person, was subject within the inspection teams, the instructions of Halilovic, of course, because Halilovic was the leader of that inspection team, Dzankovic was subject to his instructions. But Jasarevic commenting upon Mr. Dzankovic's position described him as a free shooter --
